item.title: Trump blasts Spain migrant surge as 'catastrophe,' warns US could face worse if Democrats regain power
item.description: President Donald Trump said during a Cabinet meeting that similar scenes of migrants flooding into Spain could play out in the U.S. if Democrats gain power.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump said Friday during a Cabinet meeting that scenes of migrants flooding into Spain's enclave of Ceuta from Morocco looked like a "catastrophe," but that the U.S. could see worse in the future if Democrats regain power.

"You know, I saw Spain yesterday, and I watched the catastrophe that took place. It looks like an invasion of a country by hundreds of thousands of people. And that same thing is going to happen to us if the Republicans don't get elected," Trump said Friday at Camp David. "Except worse, much bigger, much easier to get into. Despite the fact that we have built thousands of miles of wall, which I said we were going to do. But if we didn't have that, forget it. But we have the safest border in the world. If we're not in office, our country will be invaded at levels that made Spain look small time."

"And when I watched it, I said, boy, I said, ‘I'm going to say it because I knew you were going to be at Camp David.’ And I say, ‘That's going to be a talking point for the midterms, because when you look at what happened to Spain, they don't know what to do.’ And it's happening again today," the president continued. "They're coming in by the tens of thousands. It’s just invading the country. And what that is weak law, bad management, but very liberal law. They passed a couple of laws and people read, you know, people are smart. They read from other countries, and they swam that three-mile swim or however they got in."

"But nobody's seen anything like it. That will look good compared to what's going to happen to the United States," Trump also said. "The biggest thing, the worst thing that Biden did is allowing 25 million people into our country, because many of those people are criminals. They're murderers," Trump also said. "A lot of them are gone now. We got them out. But they allowed people to come into this country that you can't allow to come into a country."

WHITE HOUSE BLASTS SPANISH GOVERNMENT AS THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS SURGE FROM MOROCCO, EMERGENCY REQUEST DENIED

Trump made similar comments to Fox News' Jacqui Heinrich earlier Friday morning.

"It’s terrible. Remember that picture. That’s going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in," Trump said.

"If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life," he warned.

U.S. border security has remained a key plank of the president's campaign and policy focus throughout his political career.

An English translation of a Friday Spanish-language post on X from Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said, "The Government will guarantee the safety of the residents of Ceuta, intensifying the presence of the Security Forces and Corps on the city's streets." The post also included a video of him delivering remarks in Spanish.

FIREBRAND REP UNLOADS ON SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER AS 'HORDES OF MILITARY AGED MEN' SWARM EUROPEAN COUNTRY

Ceuta, which is located along the northwestern African coast and borders Morocco, is not attached to mainland Spain.

"Additionally, we will deploy a physical containment barrier in the sea to facilitate repatriation at the border, in compliance with the Supreme Court ruling. We will expedite the repatriation files of the migrants who arrived irregularly. And we will maintain cooperation with the Moroccan authorities to continue fighting against the mafias that traffic in human beings," the prime minister's post added.

Around 60,000 migrants had ventured from Morocco to Ceuta over the past 24 hours, Cueta President Juan Jesús Vivas said on Friday.

At least 41 migrants lost their lives.

SPAIN DEPLOYS MILITARY AFTER THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS OVERWHELM BORDER ENCLAVE, AT LEAST 18 DEAD

Spain's interior ministry issued its own figures not long after Vivas spoke, estimating that some 50,000 individuals came from Morocco since Thursday, adding that half had already gone back to Morocco.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: WATCH: Fauci walks away when pressed on Fifth Amendment, pandemic regrets
item.description: Anthony Fauci walked away from questions about pleading the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times during Rand Paul's Senate hearing on gain-of-function research.
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Anthony Fauci declined to answer Fox News Digital's questions outside his home Thursday, walking away when asked whether he regretted pleading the Fifth Amendment during a contentious Senate hearing or his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Do you regret the way you handled the hearing, pleading the Fifth so much?" Fox News Digital asked Fauci.

Fauci’s silence came one day after he declined, on the advice of his attorneys, to answer questions before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci said in his opening statement.

The former White House COVID adviser was questioned over his response to the pandemic and his policy decisions, and was accused of funding gain-of-function research in Wuhan, China.

Paul argues Fauci’s invocation of the Fifth Amendment was unsupported because Biden pardoned him and said the committee will vote next week on a resolution to hold him in contempt of Congress.

CAN FAUCI HIDE BEHIND THE FIFTH? GAME-CHANGING BIDEN PARDON MAY NOT PROVIDE COMPLETE COVER, EXPERTS SAY

"The Fifth Amendment is to claim immunity from self-incrimination," Paul said on "The Will Cain Show" on Wednesday. "But if you've already been given immunity, you can't self-incriminate unless you lie."

Fauci also stayed silent when asked if he regrets the decisions he made as the public’s health leader during the pandemic.

"Is there anything you would do different on COVID sir?" Fox News Digital asked after Fauci refused to answer questions about his Senate hearing.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Paul released more than 1,100 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era diary entries before the hearing, arguing they revealed discrepancies between Fauci’s private notes and public statements.

One entry documented an early discussion in which several scientists considered whether features of the virus could have been deliberately inserted. Fauci subsequently publicly favored a natural origin.

Fauci also said publicly that he was not responsible for rallying schools to shut down during the pandemic. But he wrote in his diary that he influenced both New York and California government officials to lock down their state’s school systems.

Paul, with the support of other GOP senators, has announced that he is seeking contempt charges against Fauci following his refusal to answer questions in Wednesday’s hearing.

item.title: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker guarantees Democratic nominee in 2028 will be anti-Israel

item.content:encoded:

"Surely shouldn't you get on board with whoever the main candidate is?" O'Sullivan asked.

"Luckily, I don't think I'll have to make that calculation at all because there is 0% chance that whoever the elected Democrat is that wins the primary will be pro-Israel in any way, shape or form. You'll see," Piker responded.

The far-left streaming personality was recently asked about his preferred candidate for Democrats in 2028.

When asked to choose between Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., as his preferred candidate, Piker immediately selected the New York congresswoman.

Polling has shown support for Israel collapse among Democrats, and far-left candidates have won primaries across the country this year with anti-Israel platforms.

Piker made the choice at the end of a rapid-fire exercise that began with California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel. The list later included former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former Vice President Kamala Harris, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Khanna.

Piker has come under renewed scrutiny over a recent addition to his visual background during his streams.

Viewers noticed what appeared to be a framed copy of the front page of a newspaper with an image of the Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the Twin Towers in New York City.

The earliest livestream reviewed by Fox News Digital showing the newspaper in the background was broadcast on July 13. The front page appears to be The New York Times' Sept. 12, 2001, edition, which was headlined, "U.S. Attacked: Hijacked Jets Destroy Twin Towers and Hit Pentagon in Day of Terror." The X account DSA Watch posted a clip of Piker's stream, where he discussed the newspaper front page framed on the wall behind him.

"You might have noticed something, some changes behind me. I finally framed the cutie Cinderella newspaper from 9/11, the morning of 9/12… the newspaper that covered 9/11. It's now officially sitting behind me," he told viewers earlier this month.

Piker was widely criticized after saying that "America deserved 9/11" during a stream in 2019. item.title: Trump rejects Iran blame for Minnesota cyberattack, points finger at 'corrupt' political foe
item.description: Trump dismissed claims that Iranian hackers targeted Minnesota water systems, instead blaming the state's governor for what he called gross incompetence.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump dismissed speculation that Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting dozens of water systems in Minnesota, blaming instead the state’s "corrupt governor," Tim Walz, and the state he runs.

"I just want to mention that we heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack, and they blame it on Iran," he said at the start of a Cabinet meeting Friday at Camp David, Maryland.

"I don't think so. I think I blame it on Minnesota because they're grossly incompetent," Trump said. "There was a cyberattack of 30 water plants, and I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, oh, is Iran? Iran should be so lucky. Iran's got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota."

Trump’s dismissal puts him at odds with a preliminary assessment reportedly shared by U.S. and state officials and comes days after federal agencies warned that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting the same kinds of systems. Iranian involvement and poor cybersecurity are not mutually exclusive: previous Iranian-linked attacks on U.S. water facilities exploited internet-connected equipment protected by default or nonexistent passwords.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBES MINNESOTA OVER 'TRANSGENDER DOLLS' IN SCHOOLS, BUT STATE DISPUTES STORY

Trump has repeatedly attacked 2024 vice presidential candidate Walz over widespread fraud in Minnesota’s state-administered social services programs.

Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee, abandoned his bid for a third term in January amid mounting scrutiny of his administration’s handling of the schemes. Walz has not been accused of participating in the fraud.

Minnesota IT Services said the "coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems" Sunday and Monday, but the Minnesota Department of Health is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage."

U.S. and state officials and others familiar with the incident told The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the cyberattack.

Minnesota IT Services said it has not determined yet whether a "specific actor" was responsible for the attack and the probe remains active.

The attacks disrupted automated operations in several communities.

Malicious software temporarily shut down controls for the well and water treatment plant in Braham, while Plymouth and South St. Paul shifted some operations to manual control. Officials reported no known threat to drinking water.

Federal agencies warned just days before the Minnesota attacks that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting the computerized controls used by water systems, power facilities and local governments. The agencies said the campaign had already disrupted operations at some facilities and caused financial losses. Investigators assessed that the hackers were seeking to cause disruption inside the U.S.

Iran has targeted American water infrastructure before.

In 2023, hackers affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps breached programmable controllers at several U.S. water and wastewater facilities, according to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The hackers generally exploited equipment that was exposed to the internet and still used default or nonexistent passwords. The affected utilities moved some operations offline, and no drinking water was compromised.

In an earlier case, the Justice Department charged an Iranian hacker with repeatedly accessing the control system of a small dam in Rye, New York, in 2013. Prosecutors said the intrusion would have allowed him to operate the dam’s sluice gate remotely, but the gate had been manually disconnected for maintenance at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment.

Fox News' Gregory Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

item.title: NFL analyst Tony Romo placed on leave by CBS Sports following drunk driving arrest in Wisconsin
item.description: J.J. Watt replaces Tony Romo as CBS Sports' lead NFL analyst indefinitely after Romo's OWI arrest and leave from the network's No. 1 broadcast team.
item.content:encoded:
Tony Romo, arrested a week ago on charges related to operating a vehicle while intoxicated, has been sidelined from his role as the top NFL analyst at CBS, the network announced Friday morning.

"Tony Romo is on leave from his role at CBS Sports until further notice," CBS Sports said in a statement.

It is unclear to what degree the leave was negotiated with Romo – whether he agreed or even requested it so that he could manage the legal and personal ramifications of his arrest.

TONY ROMO ARRESTED IN MILWAUKEE FOR ALLEGED OWI OFFENSE: REPORT

It is possible Romo wanted this. It is also possible it was foisted upon him by his employer, who saw putting Romo on air during this time as a bad strategy.

The network is replacing Romo with former Houston Texans defensive lineman J.J. Watt as its lead analyst. Watt will work with play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on the No. 1 CBS announcing team.

The first CBS game scheduled this NFL season is a preseason matchup between the Cincinnati Bengals and Philadelphia Eagles on Aug. 28. That primetime game begins at 8 p.m.

NFL EMPLOYEES' TROUBLING DRIVING INCIDENTS MOUNT

CBS is poised for an extended Romo leave, according to an industry source who added that Watt has been told his addition to the No. 1 announcing team is indefinite.

Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office deputies stopped Romo on Interstate 43 after observing what their report described as unsafe passing. Authorities said Romo displayed signs of impairment, performed poorly on field sobriety tests and refused a preliminary breath test.

Deputies also reported finding an open bottle of alcohol inside Romo's vehicle. Romo was cited for first-offense OWI, unsafe passing and having an open intoxicant in a motor vehicle before being booked and later released pending a September court appearance.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Romo, 46, became CBS Sports' lead NFL game analyst on April 4, 2017, the same day he announced his retirement from the NFL after the Dallas Cowboys released him.

CBS immediately announced that Romo would replace Phil Simms, who had served as the network's No. 1 game analyst since 1998. Romo was paired with Nantz and Wolfson on CBS's top NFL broadcast team.

item.title: Keep your eyes trained on this Big Ten sleeper to make some conference noise in 2026
item.description: Jedd Fisch's Washington Huskies rank in the top 15 in returning production with quarterback Demond Williams Jr. leading a favorable schedule.
item.content:encoded:
With Big Ten Media Days wrapping up on Thursday, talking season is officially in the books, and if I may be so bold, thank GOD!

Now we can finally look ahead to the start of college football season, and with that, the picture of 2026 as a whole starts to come into focus.

Speaking of the Big Ten, after looking through the conference's predicted order of finish, I have zeroed in on one dark horse that my shock a ton of people this coming season.

ONE OF THESE EIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS WILL BE HOISTING THE NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP TROPHY IN 2026

I have been seeing the USC Trojans getting a lot of love as a "sleeper" in the Big Ten conference, and while I really like how 2026 is shaping up for Lincoln Riley and the Men of Troy, they were picked to finish fourth by the media.

I wanted something a little more exciting, and after scrolling a little deeper down the list of teams, I think I may have found my Big Ten sleeper.

All the way down at seventh – not a doormat but certainly not a favorite either – you'll find the Washington Huskies, and I absolutely love what they have going on heading into the season.

INDIANA'S CURT CIGNETTI ROASTS THE SEC AS ESPN STARTS THEIR PROMOTIONAL CAMPAIGN ALREADY: 'WE DON'T WHINE'

For Washington, it starts at the top with head coach Jedd Fisch.

This might be my bias showing, but Fisch was my top pick for the Florida Gators when it became obvious that Lane Kiffin was heading elsewhere. I believe he's one hell of a coach, but the numbers back this up, as well.

Fisch's previous stop before arriving in Seattle was with the Arizona Wildcats, and in year one he inherited a mess of a program, bottoming out at 1-11.

INDIANA COACH CURT CIGNETTI BECOMES UNSTOPPABLE THANKS TO LATEST DEVELOPMENT ON RECRUITING TRAIL

Year two was appreciably better at 5-7, but still nothing to write home about.

In year three, however, Fisch and the Wildcats were the talk of college football, shocking everyone with a 10-3 record and putting players like QB Noah Fifita and wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan on the map.

Surprisingly, Fisch didn't stick around for another year with Fifita and McMillan in Tucson, opting to take over for the newly departed Kalen DeBoer at Washington.

The cupboard was left pretty bare for Fisch when he touched down in the Pacific Northwest, as the new Huskies head coach had to replace 20 of his 22 starters from the team that went to the national championship game just a season prior.

Fisch showed his chops once again, guiding the Huskies to a 6-7 record and a berth in the Sun Bowl despite having to patch together an entire team from scratch.

After a 9-4 season and a bowl win in 2025, it's safe to see why I'm so optimistic about the Huskies given Fisch's track record of ascending each subsequent season.

Washington didn't take a ton of players in the transfer portal, and while some might view that as a negative, I think it's a sign of things stabilizing for the team.

The Huskies rank in the top 15 nationally in returning production at 65%, just a tick under Oregon and UCLA for tops in the Big Ten and certainly a far cry from his first season in Seattle.

The biggest reason for optimism among those returning starters is quarterback Demond Williams Jr.

After spot duty and a few starts in 2024, Williams blossomed into a legitimate threat both through the air and on the ground and was one of the most coveted players in the transfer portal before he opted to return to Washington for his junior year.

Other talented returning starters include offensive tackle Drew Azzopardi and safety Alex McLaughlin, both of whom are generating plenty of buzz in the preseason.

The schedule sets up very nicely for the Huskies, too, as they play five of their first six games within the friendly confines of Husky Stadium and won't leave the Pacific Time Zone until mid-October.

They also avoid Ohio State and Michigan while they get both Indiana and Penn State at home this year.

If you need a Big Ten darkhorse to ride with in 2026, I suggest you look no further than the Washington Huskies.

They have the coaching, the returning production at key positions, and the schedule to be a real threat this coming season.

Buy stock in Fisch and company now, because it won't be getting any cheaper.

item.title: Critics rage at rogue red-state senators for blocking Todd Blanche after backing Biden's pick
item.description: John Cornyn and Thom Tillis face fierce Republican backlash for blocking Todd Blanche's confirmation after both voted to confirm Merrick Garland.
item.content:encoded:
Republicans online are raging at two turncoat red-state Senators who are obstructing the confirmation of Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to take on the role permanently after just a few years ago endorsing and voting for former President Joe Biden's pick for the same position.

Outgoing Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., have both vowed not to confirm Blanche, despite backing former Attorney General Merrick Garland when Biden tapped him for the role. At the time of Garland's confirmation, both Republican senators characterized the polarizing figure as experienced and bipartisan, and swore he would be a responsible leader of Department of Justice (DOJ).

But during Biden's presidency, Garland oversaw a DOJ that twice indicted Trump, prosecuted pro-life activists under an obscure federal law and investigated traditional Catholics as potential violent extremists, all moves that conservative critics argue were politically motivated.

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

The perceived hypocrisy in Cornyn and Tillis was not lost on online critics who raged against their move to block Blanche for ascending to the Attorney General post as Trump threatened to pull his nomination until after the two Republicans are out of office in January.

"Both Tillis and Cornyn voted to confirm Garland and then sat back idly as a weaponized DOJ/FBI destroyed lives for purely partisan reasons," said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project. "The Anti-Weaponization Fund would begin to right the wrongs and that is why they oppose Todd Blanche. Pitiful."

Columnist Mark Davis also recalled the pair voting for Garland.

"As John Cornyn and Thom Tillis high-five each other in their attempt to block Trump’s AG pick Todd Blanche, never forget that they both voted to confirm Merrick Garland," he said.

"Pretty incredible that John Cornyn is proving us exactly correct about him after he lost his primary by close to 30 points. Everything we said about him is being proven 1000 percent correct," said Breitbart's Matthew Boyle.

Prominent commentator Julie Kelly mocked Cornyn for a 2021 speech he made in favor of Garland's confirmation.

"Flashback to when John Cornyn gave a full throated endorsement of Merrick Garland so he could 'depoliticize' the DOJ," she said, adding video of the speech.

A popular commentary account that boasts nearly three million followers posted the same video.

"This is exactly why Texas republicans [sic] fired incumbent Cornyn," the account said. "He votes to approve Garland but refuses to support Todd Blanche. Merrick Garland was the most corrupt lawfare AG is U.S. history."

CORNYN PREDICTS TRUMP MIDTERM 'DISASTER,' THEN 'THE MOST MISERABLE TWO YEARS OF HIS LIFE'

During Garland's confirmation, the Texas senator, who lost his primary election in a runoff landslide in June, raved about Garland whom he painted as an objective, apolitical nominee.

"This morning I had a very good conversation with judge Merrick Garland, who President Biden has nominated for attorney general," Cornyn said at the time. "Judge Garland's extensive legal experience makes him well-suited to lead the Department of Justice, and I appreciated his commitment to keep politics out of the Justice Department."

WATCH: GOP HOLDOUT REJECTS TRUMP THREAT AS AG NOMINEE STANDOFF EXPLODES

Tillis said at the time of Garland's confirmation that Garland, "has an outstanding record serving our country and has a deep understanding of the law," raving about his reputation for "bipartisanship" and later adding that he had "no doubt he will serve with integrity" and "will respect the constitutional rights and liberties of all Americans."

But earlier this month, the North Carolina senator warned Blanche not to make the same "mistakes that the Biden administration did" if confirmed, referring to the politicization that he Garland would avoid.

Tillis decided last year not to run for reelection. Cornyn, meanwhile, lost his Republican primary race against former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was backed by President Trump.

Trump on Thursday blasted the two outgoing Republican senators.

"Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it! He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time," Trump said on TRUTH Social. "However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting."

Fox News Digital reached out to Cornyn and Tillis' offices but did not hear back by time of publication.

item.title: Stephen A. Smith only speaks up about important societal issues only when it's politically acceptable

item.content:encoded:
Stephen A. Smith is a politician as much as a sports media personality nowadays. There has been talk about him running for president, he’s cozied up to politicians and has made frequent appearances on political news channels. "It turns out that, no matter what the truth is behind all of this, Kyrie Irving did nobody wrong. We did him wrong. I did him wrong. And for that, I’m sincerely sorry, Smith stated.

DID THE BIDEN ADMINISTRATION PURPOSEFULLY IGNORE COVID VACCINE SIDE EFFECTS?

item.title: Smithsonian America 250 exhibit features 3x more liberal items than conservative ones
item.description: The Smithsonian's America 250th anniversary exhibit features nearly two dozen items for liberal causes but just seven representing conservatism.
item.content:encoded:
A Smithsonian exhibit designed to commemorate America’s 250th birthday displays numerous objects linked to key points in the nation’s history, though it provides relatively little representation of Christianity or conservatism despite ample coverage for LGBT rights and racial justice movements, among other liberal causes, a Fox News Digital review of the exhibit's online catalog found.

In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness is an exhibit curated by the Smithsonian Institution with the aim of displaying 250 objects that help to tell the story of America from the 1700s to the present. Among these objects are historically significant items, such as a compass from the 1806 Lewis and Clark expedition, a dress belonging to Dolly Madison, Abraham Lincoln’s hat and the desk the Declaration of Independence was written on.

Also included in the exhibit, according to an online catalog published by the Smithsonian, are a number of objects with clear ties to modern liberal politics, such as a pink "p-ssy hat" worn by a participant of the 2017 Women's March, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s gavel, monarch butterfly wings worn by an illegal immigrant activist and a typewriter belonging to liberal writer Maya Angelou.

Next to Angelou’s typewriter is a picture of a 1970s drag queen "wearing an off-the-shoulder shimmery gown," according to a visual description of the exhibit published by the Smithsonian.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

The exhibit’s selections are drawing scrutiny as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans challenge the Smithsonian’s portrayal of American history around the nation’s 250th anniversary.

Fox News Digital reviewed the Smithsonian’s online catalog and grouped objects according to the movements, causes and institutions identified in the museum’s descriptions, finding seven tied to conservative movements, compared with nearly two dozen tied to causes including LGBT rights, abortion access, racial justice, organized labor and Democratic politics.

The apparent domination of liberal causes in an exhibit designed to celebrate the contributions of all Americans to the nation's history could further inflame conservative criticisms of the museum.

While the exhibit examines how left-of-center individuals and movements shaped American history, conservatives have less representation.

Just seven items representing conservative movements — a MAGA hat, a Tea Party placard, a pro-life sign, a dress worn by Melania Trump, a sign opposing the feminist-backed Equal Rights Amendment, a Ronald Reagan campaign T-shirt and a National Rifle Association button — are presented by the Smithsonian, according to its online catalog.

By comparison, the same catalog shows that liberal causes — such as LGBT rights, farm-worker rights, abortion access, racial justice, environmentalism, labor unions and the Democratic Party — collectively have nearly two dozen items representing them.

THE WAR ON AMERICA’S JUDEO-CHRISTIAN ROOTS THREATENS EVERYTHING WE SHARE

Among those, the Smithsonian chose four total items representing the gay rights movement, for example. 

That wasn't far behind the six it curated to represent Christianity, including items from churches and a Bible, per its catalog. Christianity historically was America's dominant faith, influencing nearly all aspects of life, though it has declined in prominence in recent decades.

Even the items representing Christianity, however, include undertones of racial justice. 

A pew from a Black Presbyterian church, for example, is accompanied by a description of its pastor's racial activism. The one Bible on display as part of the exhibit, meanwhile, discusses the owner's anti-slavery sentiments.

Other religions, such as Judaism, with a Seder plate and a Hanukkah lamp, and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day saints, colloquially known as Mormons, with a plate depicting one of their temples, received representation as well.

Among the LGBT artifacts displayed by the Smithsonian is a red tie that belonged to the late lesbian activist Carmen Vázquez. A description for the item notes that she described it as her "seduction necktie."

"Vázquez was born in Puerto Rico and grew up in New York City. After College, she lived in San Francisco for many years, honing her political understanding of immigrant rights and women’s and public health," the online exhibit description continues. "Her endless energy for LGBTQ+ rights and justice for all, and her work, writing, and speeches ensured the safety and capacity to thrive of countless people across the United States."

LGBTQ PRESS CONFERENCE AT TRACK MEET INVOLVING TRANS ATHLETE DESCENDS INTO CHAOS, POLICE SUMMONED

The online catalog also shows that nearly two-dozen items displayed at the exhibit are related to recent waves of Asian and Latino immigration. Earlier migrant groups such as the Irish, French and Italians, received just one entry each.

One display dedicated to recent immigrants is a soccer ball donated by the founder of the Fugees soccer team for refugee children in Clarkston, Georgia, describing how the group "overcame anti-immigrant backlash."

The Smithsonian did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital. However, comments made by the National Museum of American History's director provide some insight as to why curators made the decisions they did when selecting items for the exhibit.

"How do you structure a commemoration, celebration and time for reflection?" Anthea Hartig, the museum’s director, told British newspaper The Guardian. "What we landed on were those moments where individuals or communities had fought for recognition and advocated for their own sense of identity and self in their role in creating and becoming a part of the United States. But we also wanted to do the playful."

Beyond items of political or ideological significance, the exhibit also makes an effort to showcase historical changes to domestic life, technology and pop culture through the display of everyday objects.

Various household appliances from different points in American history, props from the Star Wars movies, currency spanning hundreds of years, instruments belonging to famous musicians, technological advancements in areas such as video games and telecommunications and sports paraphernalia, like hockey gloves worn during the 1980 "miracle on ice" Olympic match against the Soviet Union, are all on display.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: America needs a museum for COVID madness
item.description: A proposed Museum of the COVID Lockdowns would memorialize everything from nursing home deaths to remote learning failures and church closures.
item.content:encoded:
Not long after 9/11, I was on St. Mark’s Place in Lower Manhattan when a bartender told me about a makeshift memorial and museum that had been set up nearby. That night, my wife and I walked into a strange, candle-lit, abandoned school filled with newly made paintings, sculptures and even debris. The whole thing was staggeringly beautiful and deeply human.

Watching the entire COVID narrative of 2020 blowing up with the disgrace of Dr. Anthony "Take the Fifth," Fauci, this week, I could not help but think that the COVID lockdowns require their own museum, preferably in Washington, D.C., so that we can finally, truly understand what happened to us.

Despite the bluster of some Republican politicians, it seems clear that there will be little to no legal reckoning for the lies about everything from COVID’s origin, to the efficacy of masking or distancing, to the constant shifting stories about the vaccines. But that doesn't mean we can’t have a physical reckoning.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

In my own vision of the Museum of the COVID Lockdowns, visitors will be given two masks to put on for safety upon entry, and cameras will monitor whether patrons touch their own faces during their visit, with loud sirens announcing violations.

I did a bit of crowdsourcing on social media to see what kinds of exhibits people think belong in this museum. There was no shortage of responses, ranging from hilarious to tragic.

Among the more light-hearted entry suggestions were interpretive dance TikTok videos from teachers and nurses, and photos of socially distant concertgoers sitting in little isolated circles. My favorite suggestion, from a New York liquor distiller, was "A bottle of hand sanitizer my distillery made along with the news article about the FDA trying to fine distillers for making it."

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

As far as the darker side of the lockdowns go, people came up with a sea of sins, everything from images of grandparents dying alone in nursing homes, to charts showing how many cancer screenings never happened, to the frustration of students locked in pointless remote learning.

At this museum, we will also see the stories of courage and freedom, brave church goers who broke the law to worship, speakeasy New York City bars defying lockdown and even a crazy, freezingly cold, Canadian trucker protest against vaccine mandates.

Such a memorial is needed for the same reason it has been since the pyramids were erected, lest we forget the dead. It was 18th Century philosopher Giambattista Vico who argued that the very term "human," comes from the root word "humando," which means "to bury." Vico says humans are the animals who bury their dead, but we are also the animals who remember them.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

The Museum of the COVID Lockdowns will not just serve as a memorial for those who succumbed to the Chinese virus, but also to those who needlessly perished as a result of ham-fisted overclosures, which, according to former White House COVID Task Force member Dr. Deborah Birx, were overtly politically motivated in blue states.

An advantage that a museum has over retribution is permanence. I can understand those who, after seeing Fauci squirm on the Senate hearing hot seat, or having read the lies he bragged about in his diary, want his last few years spent in jail, but such punishment would fade much faster than the stonework of an institution.

More than anything, a Museum of the COVID Lockdowns would serve as a warning, insurance that we never again are asked to rat out neighbors giving haircuts in backyards, or allow people to go weeks without so much as touching another human being.

What we remember will always be in the past, but the act of remembering will always be in the present, and future generations must know what we allowed to happen so that it never happens again.

In the 25 years since 9/11, I have looked online in vain for any evidence of the impromptu museum that sprang up in the East Village in the face of brutal tragedy. But I know it was real, I know it was organic and I know that it helped.

One-hundred years from now, somewhere on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., our great-grandchildren should have a place to see and understand our folly, to learn what happens when a society trades freedom for the illusion of perfect safety.

The COVID lockdowns of 2020 were the most insane, wrongheaded and inexplicable events of our lifetimes, and it is time that we tell that story, in brick and mortar, so that our progeny do not ever make the same tragic mistakes.

item.content:encoded:
A liberal-led federal appeals court handed President Donald Trump two immigration victories Wednesday, reversing separate district court orders that had delayed the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for migrants from South Sudan and Ethiopia.

The judgments from the First Circuit Court of Appeals come after U.S. District Judges Brian Murphy and Patti Saris issued back-to-back orders temporarily blocking the Trump administration's termination of TPS for Ethiopia and South Sudan, respectively, late last week. The rulings drew sharp criticism from legal experts and Trump administration officials, who called the judges "rogue" and argued their decisions defied the Supreme Court.

The three-judge First Circuit panel consisted of Judges Julie Rikelman and Seth Aframe, both appointed by President Joe Biden, and Judge Joshua Dunlap, who was appointed by President Donald Trump.

BIDEN JUDGE BLOCKING ETHIOPIAN DEPORTATIONS DESPITE SCOTUS RULING CLASHED WITH ICE BEFORE

SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS

In nearly identical rulings, the majority liberal panel found that the lower court judges' orders conflicted with the Supreme Court's decision in Mullin v. Doe, which held that courts cannot block TPS terminations based on non-constitutional claims.

"Mullin held that 'the TPS statute's judicial-review bar applies to all non-constitutional claims' challenging the Secretary of Homeland Security's determination with respect to the termination of a TPS designation," the judges wrote.

Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan told Fox News Digital that the First Circuit correctly applied the precedent established by the Supreme Court.

"These are clear wins for President Trump following his big win at the U.S. Supreme Court, explaining that district courts are not supposed to second guess TPS terminations, and even as this plays out, we're moving towards the end of this litigation because district courts should not be hearing these disputes, and that's what the Supreme Court said," Wessan told Fox News Digital.

SUPREME COURT'S LATEST IMMIGRATION RULING WILL CAUSE AMERICANS TO 'DIE AND SUFFER' ATTORNEY WARNS

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson welcomed the rulings as "a win for the rule of law and common sense."

"Temporary Protected Status is exactly that—temporary," the spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent."

The lawsuits were brought by African Communities Together, a New York-based immigrant advocacy organization that serves as the lead plaintiff in both cases, alongside individual TPS recipients from Ethiopia and South Sudan. The plaintiffs argue DHS unlawfully ended the protections in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act and the Constitution, alleging the agency failed to properly assess conditions in the two countries and that the decisions were motivated by racial discrimination.

Murphy and Saris temporarily blocked the Trump administration from terminating TPS last week, issuing procedural orders to preserve the status quo while they considered whether the plaintiffs should be permitted to amend their complaints to pursue renewed constitutional claims.

DHS EVISCERATES MEDIA FOR ‘ABSOLUTE ABSURDITY’ OVER CONCERN ABOUT ‘WORST OF THE WORST’ ACTIVIST JUDGES LIST

While the Supreme Court's decision in Mullin v. Doe foreclosed most statutory challenges to TPS terminations, it left open the possibility that courts could consider claims alleging constitutional violations.

However, Wessan said the district judges were operating outside the "legal bounds" by blocking the TPS terminations before any constitutional claims had been established.

"If they want to let the plaintiffs amend their complaint, they're allowed to do that, but in the meantime, TPS is over," Wessan told Fox News Digital.

The First Circuit's decisions mark the latest setback for Murphy and Saris after the Trump administration accused both judges of effectively sidestepping the Supreme Court's June ruling. After Murphy's order, DHS General Counsel James Percival wrote on X that the district judge was engaged in "mutiny against the Supreme Court," while he described Saris' ruling as "open defiance" of the justices' decision.

Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Murphy and Saris for comment.

item.title: Monica Lewinsky has one request for critics nearly 30 years after White House scandal
item.description: Monica Lewinsky wishes critics would get new jokes after nearly three decades, sharing on a podcast how she reshaped public perception of her own story.
item.content:encoded:
Monica Lewinsky has evolved since the White House scandal – and she hopes critics one day can, too.

Lewinsky, 53, credited time and patience as her saving graces while reflecting on challenges from her past during an appearance on the "All the Cool Girls" podcast.

"I think that coming into my 50s was amazing and just the shedding of worries," she told co-hosts Laura Brown and Kristina O'Neill.

MONICA LEWINSKY'S LINDSEY GRAHAM TRIBUTE DRAWS CRITICISM AND PRAISE FOR PLACING PEOPLE OVER PARTY: EXPERT

"I mean that whole … joke about 'I don't give anymore f---s,' and it's like you really start to give fewer and fewer f---s, and you settle into acceptance in a way that has been really reassuring for me."

Unlike the critics, the podcast host moved on from past discretions to reclaim not only her life, but also her own story.

"In terms of the people who still have old, old beliefs, I wish they would get some new jokes because, I mean, 30 years of the same jokes, Jesus," she said. "Or 28 years. We're not at 30 yet."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Lewinsky was 21 years old when she began an unpaid internship at the White House in July 1995. She turned 22 that summer, and her sexual relationship with former President Bill Clinton, who was 49 at the time, began in November 1995.

It was only after she confided in a Pentagon co-worker, Linda Tripp – who secretly recorded their conversations, which were then used in Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against Clinton – when the affair became public fodder.

During a January 1998 White House news conference, Clinton famously denied the affair, and stated, "I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky," and Lewinsky subsequently went into hiding due to public humiliation.

The subsequent impeachment trial against the 42nd president began in January 1999 and ended Feb. 12. While Clinton was impeached by the house, he was acquitted of perjury and obstruction of justice charges.

While the scandal made headlines for years, Lewinsky only truly began reclaiming her identity in the last decade.

"I feel really grateful. I'm really grateful, and I'm excited," she said. "It's when I step away, and I look at my own story objectively – or as objectively as one can – it is pretty extraordinary to still be here, like physically still here, and to have been able to help shape how people see me more and understand me more and connect with me in ways that are meaningful. It's bonkers."

Themes surrounding authority and control have remained a constant in Lewinsky's life post scandal.

"I think of power in two different ways. There's the power that someone has and they use, that impacts other people's power," Lewinsky explained to Fox News Digital earlier this year.

"Then there's the power that someone has in connection to themselves and that's a lot more like strength."

She added, "People often think of resilience as being linear, and it is so much more like a spiral. You will move forward, you'll go back, and move forward ... you'll go back, and I think it's, again, people have to be patient with themselves."

item.title: Why the under on runs looks like the smart baseball play when Pirates visit the Reds tonight
item.description: Paul Skenes and Hunter Greene face off as the Pittsburgh Pirates visit the Cincinnati Reds, with the under eight runs emerging as the smart play.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday did not go as expected. I lost one game between the Giants and Padres as Robbie Ray spun a gem in what could be his last start for the squad. Sometimes you run into that, and all you can do is tip your cap to the other team. I'll suck it up and move on, and hopefully get some of that money back here today as we play the Pirates vs. the Reds.

The Pittsburgh Pirates seem to be in a similar cycle this season. They have one step forward and then one back. I suppose the good news is that they aren't going one step forward and two steps backward. They are exactly at .500 coming into today's game, sitting at 55-55 for the year. The final 52 games of the season will tell the story of whether this year is successful or not. Maybe that's harsh, because this still should be a step-forward season, and one they can use for momentum moving forward.

I've written about the importance of Pittsburgh being aggressive in using this window for them to make a consistently good team. If they don't, guys like today's starter, Paul Skenes, will start looking for ways off the team. Skenes is 9-9 for the season with a 3.65 ERA and a 1.06 WHIP. This is the worst season of his young career, but all of his numbers are 31st in the Majors or better. He has been worse on the road than at home, but not terrible. This has been a tough month for Skenes; he has allowed 17 earned runs in 27.2 innings of work. He has faced the Reds twice this season and allowed five earned runs in 10 innings of work.

The Cincinnati Reds took a step back this season after making the postseason. They started the season hot out of the gate. This team was 20-11 after April came to an end. Since then, they have gone 30-46. To start May, they lost eight consecutive games and went 4-13 to start the month. To start the second half of the season, they've gone 8-5. Perhaps the All-Star Break is what the team needed to make some adjustments.

There is more than enough time to make a run at the postseason, but they'll need to get some better performances from their pitching staff. The Reds do have some good pitchers, so the adjustments can be made. Today's starter, Hunter Greene, is one of the better young arms in the league, but he has struggled since he came into their rotation in early July. He has allowed 17 earned runs in 21.2 innings this season. In fairness to him, he has two quality starts and two disasters. Pirates hitters are batting .200 against him over 55 at-bats.

We have two aces on the mound, guys who have, or could someday, win Cy Young awards. However, neither has been exactly impressive when it comes to consistency. Skenes has struggled all month. Greene has allowed 14 earned runs in two starts, and three earned runs in his other two. Which version of these pitchers is showing up?

The Pirates haven't been playing great baseball lately, so it is really hard to back them, even with Skenes on the mound. The Reds have been terrible at home — 24-30. I think the smarter option here is to take the under eight runs. Both teams know the importance of this game, and both starters will know how crucial it is to give their team a chance. item.title: Investigators believe Iranian hackers are likely behind cyberattack on Minnesota water systems: report
item.description: More than 30 Minnesota water systems were hit by a coordinated cyberattack that officials say was likely orchestrated by Iranian hackers, a report said.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. investigators believe a cyberattack that targeted dozens of water systems in Minnesota this week likely was orchestrated by Iranian hackers, a report said.

Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) said the "coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems" on Sunday and Monday, but the Minnesota Department of Health is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage."

U.S. and state officials and others familiar with the incident told The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the cyberattack.

The newspaper reported that three state officials briefed on an investigation into the cyberattack said the tradecraft used and the absence of a ransom demand led analysts to initially determine Iran was involved. Officials also cautioned that the assessment could change as more data is collected by investigators, according to the newspaper.

However, President Donald Trump said during a Cabinet meeting Friday that he would "blame it on Minnesota and the governor."

"Today, I just want to mention that, we heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack, and they blame it on Iran. I don't think so. I think I blame it on Minnesota because they're grossly incompetent. There was a cyberattack of 30 water plants, and I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota," Trump said, referencing Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat. "They like to say, 'oh it's Iran.' Iran should be so lucky. Iran's got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota."

IRAN-LINKED HACKERS TARGET US MEDICAL TECH COMPANY

The FBI said earlier in a statement to Fox News Digital on Friday that it is "aware of recent public reporting around Water and Wastewater sectors."

"The FBI and our interagency partners are fully engaged to protect critical infrastructure and we remain well-equipped to protect against cyber threats of all varieties," the FBI added.

The New York Times reported that the hackers targeted infrastructure used to manage and monitor water towers operated by municipal governments.

The mayor of the city of Braham, Nate George, said on Monday, a "plant operator found that the water tower was calling for water, but the well was not operating."

"After learning that similar problems were occurring in at least four other Minnesota communities, Braham staff determined that the plant’s computerized control system had been compromised," he continued.

"Public works isolated the affected system, restored a backup, and restarted the plant within approximately 90 minutes. While the plant was offline, residents continued receiving water from the city’s water tower. City administration temporarily requested that residents conserve water to prevent the tower’s limited supply from being exhausted," George added.

LIVE UPDATES ON IRAN WAR: TRUMP ANNOUNCES HAMAS DISARMAMENT DEAL WHILE SAUDI ARABIA LAUNCHES RED SEA DEFENSE COALITION

In a statement shared with Fox News Digital, MNIT noted that "the investigation remains active, and Minnesota has not attributed the activity to a specific actor."

MNIT said it "continues to collaborate with federal, state, local, Tribal, and private-sector partners to investigate the attack, support affected communities, and strengthen the security of Minnesota's critical infrastructure."

"Cyberattacks against critical infrastructure require a coordinated, whole-of-government response," John Israel, MNIT assistant commissioner and Minnesota chief information security officer, said in a statement. "MNIT is working side by side with our partners to share intelligence, support affected communities, and help utilities restore operations safely while strengthening defenses against future attacks."

Israel told the Times that the breach was first detected Sunday and that hackers targeted 36 municipal water systems.

"Minnesota was one of the early detectors of this, but we’re seeing that this same threat activity has likely been occurring in other states throughout the nation," he was quoted as saying.

Nick Andersen, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) acting director, told the newspaper that the agency was aware of "multiple potential incidents affecting local water utilities."

In the days leading up to the incident, CISA issued an advisory warning U.S. organizations of "ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber activity targeting internet-connected operational technology (OT) devices."

"Iranian cyber actors continue to target U.S. critical infrastructure, and the FBI is committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing costs on those responsible," Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division said in the advisory.

It stated that a "group of Iranian-affiliated actors" has "targeted devices spanning multiple U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, including Water and Wastewater Systems, Energy and Government Services and Facilities, to include local municipalities."

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) also issued an advisory on Thursday "to warn critical infrastructure asset owners and operators that malicious cyber actors are conducting cyber attacks targeting Operational Technology devices."

"Since 27 July 2026, Water and Wastewater Sector utility companies in at least seven states have reported incidents to the FBI, and some of that activity degraded water operations," it added.

item.title: Ryan Gosling's family-first philosophy reshaped his Hollywood career: experts
item.description: From "Barbie" to "Ghost Rider," Ryan Gosling's pivot toward blockbuster franchises traces back to a deliberate family-first philosophy he embraced as a dad.
item.content:encoded:
Ryan Gosling is officially joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Ghost Rider, marking the latest chapter in a career evolution that the actor has linked directly to fatherhood.

Earlier this month, Gosling, 45, made a surprise appearance during Marvel Studios' panel at San Diego Comic-Con where it was announced that he will be starring as the titular motorcycle-riding supernatural hero in a standalone "Ghost Rider" movie slated for release in 2028.

Gosling's casting comes as the three-time Oscar nominee continues to embrace blockbuster franchises after spending years building his reputation in some of Hollywood's darkest, most critically acclaimed dramas.

MARVEL STAR VINCENT D’ONOFRIO SAYS HE ‘CAN’T DO’ KINGPIN TRANSFORMATION ANYMORE

The actor has previously shared that his pivot toward lighter, more mainstream projects was intentional, explaining that his priorities changed after becoming a parent. Gosling shares daughters Esmeralda, 11, and Amada, 10, with his longtime partner, Eva Mendes, 52.

During a 2024 interview with The Wall Street Journal, Gosling said he avoids psychologically heavy roles because he wants to be emotionally present for Mendes and their daughters.

"I don’t really take roles that are going to put me in some kind of dark place," Gosling said. "This moment is what I feel like trying to read the room at home and feel like what is going to be best for all of us. The decisions I make, I make them with Eva, and we make them with our family in mind first."

‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STAR SADIE ROBERTSON HUFF ADMITS ‘FEARS’ OVER PUTTING HER KIDS ON REALITY TV

While speaking with Fox News Digital, PR expert Sarah Schmidt shared her view that Gosling's family-first approach has reshaped not only the types of roles he is taking, but the purpose behind them.

"He began picking lighter roles to keep his mood stable for his family and also create art that they can be a part of," the president of Interdependence PR said.

Paul Dergarabedian, head of Marketplace Trends for Rentrak, said Gosling's evolving priorities reflect a broader pattern among actors whose careers change alongside their personal lives.

"It does feel as though he is gravitating toward movies that his kids could actually see and enjoy," Dergarabedian said. "That kind of evolution is not unique as we have seen it with other actors as they get older, start families, and begin making choices that reflect where they are in life, how they see the world, and how they want to be perceived both personally and professionally."

Gosling's shift toward family-friendly entertainment signals a full-circle career moment for the actor, who made his debut as a child performer on the Disney Channel's "The All-New Mickey Mouse Club." He later appeared in the children's TV shows "Are You Afraid of the Dark?" and "Goosebumps."

During a 2011 interview with The New York Times, Gosling recalled that he decided to pursue "serious acting" at age 19. After making his mainstream breakthrough in the hit 2004 romantic drama "The Notebook," the Canada native went on to establish himself as one of Hollywood's most respected dramatic actors with critically acclaimed films, including "Half Nelson," "Blue Valentine," "Drive," "The Place Beyond the Pines," "Blade Runner 2049" and "First Man."

In recent years, Gosling has charted a different course with starring roles in audience-friendly movies including "Barbie," "The Fall Guy," and "Project Hail Mary," and his upcoming turns in "Star Wars: Starfighter" and "Ghost Rider."

Ryan McCormick, co-founder of Goldman McCormick PR, said he believes Gosling has earned the creative freedom to balance blockbuster franchises with prestige films.

"Ryan has not only built a career of acclaimed roles, those films are often box office successes," McCormick told Fox News Digital. "He has attained a rare status where he can do a sandbox film like 'Ghost Rider' and also take a dramatic or independent role without any one performance limiting his future choices."

Dergarabedian noted that Gosling's career has long defied easy categorization, citing his performances in 2011's "Crazy, Stupid, Love" and 2016's "La La Land."

"Gosling has always been far more versatile than any single role would suggest," Dergarabedian said. "He has shown he can do comedy, as he did so memorably in ‘Crazy, Stupid, Love.'"

"Of course, he proved he could carry a musical with ‘La La Land,'" he added.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Dergarabedian pointed to Gosling's starring role in Nicolas Winding Refn's "Drive" as a pivotal moment that expanded audiences' perception of him beyond romantic leads and demonstrated his ability to tackle darker, action-oriented material.

"You really cannot put Gosling in a box. He has been able to move between genres and tones with a level of ease that very few actors can match," Dergarabedian said. "All that being said, you can definitely see a shift in tone at this stage of his career."

Gosling previously shared that "La La Land" was the first project he chose that reflected his changing priorities after becoming a father. While speaking with The Wall Street Journal, Gosling recalled thinking of how Esmeralda and Amada would enjoy watching him prepare for the role.

"It was just sort of like, ‘Oh, this will be fun for them, too, because even though they’re not coming to set, we’re practicing piano every day, or we’re dancing, or we’re singing,'" Gosling said.

The philosophy carried over to 2023's "Barbie," which Gosling said resonated with his daughters, who were already immersed in the world of Barbie dolls before he signed on to play Ken.

"Their interest in Barbie and their disinterest in Ken was an inspiration," Gosling said. "I thought they were already making little movies about their Barbies on the iPad when it happened, so the fact that I was going off to work to make one too, we just felt like we were aligned."

Though some fans initially criticized Gosling's casting as Ken, arguing he was too old to portray Barbie's iconic counterpart, the actor ultimately won over audiences with a performance that became one of the film's biggest highlights. "Barbie" went on to gross more than $1.4 billion worldwide and Gosling earned an Oscar nomination for best supporting actor, cementing the film as both a commercial and critical triumph.

Schmidt told Fox News Digital that she believes the film fundamentally changed the trajectory of Gosling's career.

"Gosling proved that just because he began his career as a critically acclaimed darling does not mean that he cannot also be an international franchise and blockbuster star," she said.

"'Barbie' paved the way," Schmidt continued. "Prior to that, Gosling was a serious actor who occasionally moonlighted in a rom-com. As it turns out, Ken can carry a billion-dollar movie. He was funny and self-aware, and it did not cost him any of his hard-earned credibility."

Gosling has continued to embrace projects that his daughters can share with him. While promoting "Project Hail Mary," he revealed that Esmeralda and Amada occasionally voiced his alien co-star Rocky during rehearsals and became some of the sci-fi adventure movie's earliest viewers.

"Sometimes when I was working, and I needed to sort of switch things up or whatever, my kids would come in, and I had an earpiece in my ear, and they would talk for Rocky, so I could talk to them as Rocky," Gosling told People in March.

"And there's some moments in the movie where I'm laughing or I'm just so charmed by him, which is like, it's actually my kids talking to me and helping me out," Gosling continued.

"They've seen many cuts of this film," he added of his daughters. "They've given me many notes."

Marvel's "Ghost Rider" marks the latest chapter in the blockbuster era that Gosling has spent years building. Gosling's role as Johnny Blaze/Ghost Rider in the superhero movie will also reunite him with director Shawn Levy after the two previously collaborated on "Star Wars: Starfighter," which hits theaters in May 2027.

"Wow, is this really happening?" Gosling told the crowd at Comic-Con after being unveiled as Ghost Rider by Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige.

"As you know, this is a character I’ve wanted to play for a very long time," he said.

Schmidt told Fox News Digital that she believes Gosling has found a way to balance artistic credibility with commercial success without losing sight of the priorities that reshaped his career.

"He became a dad first, actor second," Schmidt said. "He is building a filmography legacy that his kids can be part of and proud of."

Meanwhile, Dergarabedian said he believes Gosling's recent choices have also cemented his place among Hollywood's biggest stars.

"He has become a go-to actor for huge, audience-friendly studio films and major franchises because he occupies such a unique position within the public eye," Dergarabedian said. "He has credibility, he has charm, he has range, and he has that elusive movie-star quality that is increasingly rare today."

item.title: RFK Jr takes MAHA to the kitchen with HHS cooking series promoting healthy meals for under $5
item.description: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and chef Andrew Gruel prepare crispy wild Alaskan salmon cakes in the premiere of HHS's new budget-friendly cooking series.
item.content:encoded:
Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is taking the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda from policy into the kitchen with a new government-produced cooking series designed to show Americans how to prepare healthy meals for less than $5 a serving whenever possible.

The new series, "The Real Food Show," launched Thursday on the HHS website and YouTube.

"Food should be the foundation of our health," Kennedy said in a statement announcing the series. 

"With 'The Real Food Show,' we're empowering Americans to take control of their health one meal at a time. Healthy eating doesn't have to be expensive, and cooking at home can be faster, easier and more rewarding than people think."

Each episode features Kennedy alongside "America's most celebrated chefs" preparing what HHS describes as wholesome, budget-friendly meals inspired by the principles of the MAHA movement.

The agency said recipes are designed to cost less than $5 per serving whenever practical, with an emphasis on whole ingredients and home cooking.

Celebrity chef Andrew Gruel joins Kennedy in the premiere episode, where they prepare crispy wild Alaskan salmon cakes served with an apple, white bean and greens salad.

Gruel told Fox News Digital he joined the project because he believes its mission extends far beyond teaching recipes.

"I'm excited to be part of the premiere episode because I believe the message is much bigger than a cooking show," Gruel said.

Gruel said he hopes the series encourages more Americans to cook at home after years of relying on convenience foods and helps rebuild basic cooking skills that he believes have been lost.

"My hope is that this series helps demystify cooking and shows people that preparing crave-worthy, healthy meals doesn't require professional training or expensive ingredients," Gruel said.

The recipe is intended to demonstrate that nutritious meals can be both affordable and easy to make at home.

"We talk about seafood a lot because I'm a seafood junkie, and one of the things that actually drove me into the restaurant industry was understanding people need to eat more seafood, more of the right types of seafood," Gruel said in a segment from the debut episode.

Gruel selected salmon cakes because many home cooks find seafood intimidating despite how simple it can be to prepare, he told Fox News Digital.

"Salmon is also nutrient-dense, affordable (frozen is fine) and incredibly versatile," he said. "They're a great example of how you can take a high-quality protein, combine it with a handful of simple pantry ingredients and create a meal that's both satisfying and family-friendly."

The show's goal of keeping meals under $5 per serving may surprise some shoppers amid stubborn grocery prices, but Gruel said it's achievable.

"Yes, you can absolutely make this meal for under $5 per serving, particularly when using canned or frozen wild Alaskan salmon," he said.

"One of the biggest misconceptions is that eating healthy is always more expensive, but with a few basic cooking skills and a little planning, real food is often more affordable than people think."

Gruel said he hopes viewers walk away with what he calls "kitchen confidence."

"It's not about creating more Bobby Flays," he said. "It's about helping families realize they can cook nutritious, affordable meals at home using real ingredients."
